symptom_h2: You draft property papers well and want business clients too
symptom: Your practice runs on sale deeds, title checks and registration. Families and buyers trust you with the biggest purchase of their lives. You know stamp duty, encumbrances and the exact wording a sub-registrar accepts. Your drafting is careful because property mistakes are costly.

But the same clients often own shops, offices and small companies. When they sign a vendor contract or a software agreement, they go to someone else. You already draft for a living. You want your drafting to reach the businesses those families run. The step across is shorter than it looks.
outcome_h2: Become the lawyer businesses call for commercial contracts
outcome: Commercial drafting lets you serve a client every year, not once per property. A business needs a lease for its office, contracts with vendors, an employment agreement for staff and terms for its website. You can become the lawyer on call for all of them. Repeat business work tends to pay more steadily than one-off conveyancing, and it builds on the drafting discipline you already have.
alts_h2: Three things property lawyers often try first

alts.t: Taking more conveyancing files
alts.p: More sale deeds keep the practice busy, but each client leaves after registration. That work does not create the ongoing business relationships that commercial contracts do, year after year.

alts.t: Copying a commercial format from the internet
alts.p: A downloaded format gives you clause headings. It does not tell you how a lock-in period or a service level should read for this client, so you hesitate to sign off.

alts.t: Referring business work to a corporate firm
alts.p: Referring keeps the client happy for now. It also teaches the client that a different lawyer handles their business, and that habit is hard to reverse later.

reframe_h2: You already draft. The gap is the document type.
reframe: Your skill is not the problem. You draft precise, enforceable documents every week. What is missing is practice with the clauses businesses use: service levels, limitation of liability, intellectual property and termination. A short daily routine that moves you from leases into these documents closes the gap. Your clients already trust you; they just do not know you do this work.
role_h2: What conveyancing lawyers already carry into commercial drafting
role_intro: Property work is drafting at its most careful. Every boundary, payment instalment and possession date has to be exact, or registration stops. That training is the base commercial clients want, and three parts of it transfer almost unchanged into business contracts.

role_points.t: Leases are already your territory
role_points.p: A commercial lease uses the rent, deposit and lock-in ideas you know, with added fit-out, signage and permitted use clauses. It is the natural first step.

role_points.t: You know staged payments and possession
role_points.p: Joint development agreements split built area and pay landowners in stages. Your sale deed and possession experience makes those clauses easier to draft correctly.

role_points.t: Clients already trust your signature
role_points.p: Shop owners and builders who used you for property already know your work. Offering them a lease or a vendor contract is an easy conversation to start.

artifact_intro: You start where you are strongest. The commercial lease builds on your leave and licence work. Later, the joint development agreement brings in landowners, builders and shared built area, a document many property clients will recognise.
clause: 4.1 The Tenant shall have a rent-free fit-out period of sixty days from the Handover Date. 4.2 Neither party may terminate this Lease during the first thirty-six months (the Lock-in Period), except for material breach not cured within thirty days of written notice. 4.3 After the Lock-in Period, either party may terminate on ninety days' notice.
margin_note: You know lock-ins from residential leases. A business tenant cares more about the fit-out period, so they read this clause first.

alts.t: Moot courts and essay competitions
alts.p: Moots sharpen argument and research, which is useful for court. They rarely ask you to draft a contract that a business would actually sign and use.

alts.t: Waiting for the contracts paper in final year
alts.p: The contract law paper teaches doctrine and case law. Exams test what the law says, not whether you can write a clean clause for a client.

reframe_h2: You need drafted work to show, not more marks

One document a day and a LinkedIn profile built around contracts do more for your positioning than another research task.

artifact_h2: Your first lesson is the parts of a contract
artifact_intro: The first day covers how a contract is built: parties, recitals, definitions, operative clauses, boilerplate and signatures. Once you see the structure, every later document is easier. Here is a recitals and definitions block of the kind you write first.
clause: WHEREAS the Company develops mobile software and wishes to engage the Consultant to provide design services; NOW THEREFORE the parties agree as follows. 1.1 "Deliverables" means the designs listed in Schedule A. 1.2 "Effective Date" means the date on which both parties sign this Agreement.
margin_note: In exams you define terms inside answers. In a contract, a clear definition stops an argument years later. Practise these first.

symptom_h2: You left the firm for family, but kept the lawyer's eye
symptom: You did good work at the firm. You handled agreements, sat on calls with partners and learned how deals are negotiated. That experience is still yours. Then family needed you more, and you made that choice with care.

Now you want legal work again, on terms that fit your home. Going back to firm hours may not be the answer. You still read a contract and see what is missing. That skill has not gone anywhere. It only needs a refresh and a new way to find clients.
outcome_h2: Come back as a lawyer with your own clients
outcome: Instead of a desk at a firm, you can build a drafting practice around startups and small businesses. They need co-founder agreements, employment contracts, privacy policies and vendor terms, and many prefer a lawyer they can call directly. You choose the clients and the hours. With time and steady effort, this kind of practice can pay better than a junior return to a firm.
alts_h2: Three things lawyers returning to work often try first

alts.t: Applying to firms again
alts.p: Firms value your experience but often expect the same long hours and office days. The role rarely bends around school runs or care at home, however good you are.

alts.t: Taking short review tasks online
alts.p: Short review tasks bring some income and keep you reading. They do not build a client base of your own or a reputation as the lawyer who drafts.

alts.t: Waiting until the children are older
alts.p: Waiting feels sensible, yet each month adds distance from your last draft. A little practice each day keeps your skills current without disturbing home life.

reframe_h2: Your return needs positioning, not proof that you can work
reframe: Your ability was proven at the firm. The gap is how clients find you now that you are not behind a firm's name. That is a positioning task: a fresh set of drafts, a profile that says contracts, and a clear way to reach founders. Practice and visibility close that gap; talent was never the question.

role_intro: Firm years leave habits that independent clients value highly. You know how a partner reviews a draft, how deadlines feel and how negotiations move. These carry straight into running your own drafting work from home, starting with three in particular.

role_points.t: You know how partners think

role_points.t: You have handled real negotiations
role_points.p: You have seen clauses traded on calls. That makes it easier to draft a first version that already expects what the other side will ask for.

role_points.t: You know client service
role_points.p: Firm training taught you to answer quickly, explain clearly and keep records. Startups notice those habits, especially from a lawyer working directly with them.

artifact_h2: You prepare a client questions checklist for a co-founder agreement
artifact_intro: Before you draft, you ask. One live session covers the questions to put to a client before a co-founder agreement. Your checklist becomes the first thing you send any founder, and it shows them you think ahead.
clause: 1. How is equity split today, and what is that split based on? 2. Should founder shares vest, and over what period? 3. What happens if one founder leaves within the first year? 4. Who decides on hiring, spending and new investors? 5. How will a deadlock between founders be resolved?
margin_note: At the firm, a partner asked these for you. Now you ask them yourself, and founders hear an experienced lawyer from the first call.
